Question: Describe the current responsibilities of all three teams, and explain the org changes that produced this structure, step by step.
response_text:
### Current Responsibilities of the Three Teams | Team | Primary Scope | Typical Deliverables / Activities | |------|---------------|-----------------------------------| | **Frontend Team** | **User‑facing UI/UX** – everything that runs in the browser (or native client) and directly interacts with the end‑user. | • Design & implement UI components, pages, and flows (React, Angular, Vue, etc.)
• Ensure accessibility, responsiveness, and performance of the client side
• Integrate with backend APIs (authentication, data fetching, real‑time updates)
• Maintain UI‑related tooling (build pipelines, component libraries, design systems)
• Conduct UI testing (unit, integration, visual regression, end‑to‑end)
• Work closely with product, design, and QA to iterate on features. | | **Backend Team** | **Business‑logic & API layer** – the services that expose the core domain functionality to consumers (frontend, mobile apps, third‑party partners). | • Design, develop, and maintain REST/GraphQL/gRPC APIs
• Implement core business rules, validation, transaction management
• Manage data‑access layers, ORM models, and repository patterns
• Write automated tests (unit, contract, integration) for service logic
• Handle versioning, backward compatibility, and API documentation
• Collaborate with the Platform team for runtime environments, but do **not** own the underlying infrastructure. | | **Platform Team** (carved out of Backend) | **Infrastructure, DevOps, and reliability** – the foundation that runs the services, pipelines, and observability stack. | • Provision, configure, and maintain cloud resources (Kubernetes clusters, VMs, managed services)
• Build and operate CI/CD pipelines, release automation, and deployment tooling
• Implement monitoring, logging, alerting, and tracing (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, etc.)
• Define and enforce security, networking, and compliance standards
• Manage platform‑as‑a‑service offerings (service mesh, secrets management, feature flagging)
• Provide self‑service APIs or CLIs for other teams to consume infrastructure resources. | --- ### Step‑by‑Step Evolution of the Organization | Phase | Organizational Shape | Reason for Change | Resulting Team Boundaries | |-------|----------------------|-------------------|---------------------------| | **1️⃣ Initial State – “Full‑Stack Team”** | *One single team* handled everything: UI code, business‑logic services, and the underlying infrastructure. | • Early stage, small product scope.
• Limited headcount – a single cross‑functional group could deliver end‑to‑end features quickly. | • No explicit separation; developers wore many hats (frontend, backend, ops). | | **2️⃣ First Split – “Frontend + Backend”** | *Two dedicated teams* were created:
– **Frontend Team** (UI/UX)
– **Backend Team** (APIs & business logic). | • Product grew, UI became richer and required deeper specialization (design systems, performance tuning).
• Backend services grew in complexity (multiple micro‑services, data models).
• Scaling the workforce made it practical to let people focus on a narrower domain. | • Frontend team took ownership of all client‑side code.
• Backend team took ownership of the server‑side code **and** the infrastructure needed to run those services (e.g., VMs, containers, CI pipelines). | | **3️⃣ Second Split – “Platform Team” carved out of Backend** | *Three teams* emerged:
– **Frontend** (unchanged)
– **Backend** (now only business logic & APIs)
– **Platform** (infrastructure, DevOps, reliability). | • The backend team’s workload was being pulled in two directions: writing business code *and* maintaining the underlying platform (clusters, CI/CD, monitoring).
• Operational incidents, scaling requirements, and the need for tighter security/compliance highlighted the need for a dedicated platform group.
• Creating a Platform team allowed the Backend engineers to focus purely on domain logic, while the Platform engineers could build reusable, self‑service infrastructure. | • **Backend** no longer owns any infra; it consumes Platform‑provided services (e.g., “deploy my service to the cluster”, “use the shared logging stack”).
• **Platform** becomes the internal service provider for runtime, CI/CD, observability, and security.
• **Frontend** continues to own the client‑side stack and works with Backend via the APIs the Backend team publishes. | | **4️⃣ Stabilization – Current Structure** | *Three clearly defined teams* with stable, non‑overlapping responsibilities (as listed in the table above). | • The organization now operates under “standard conditions” – no major incidents, routine maintenance, and all metrics within expected ranges.
• The separation has proven effective: faster delivery of UI features, more predictable backend releases, and higher reliability of the underlying platform. | • The three‑team model is the status‑quo, supporting ongoing growth and allowing each team to specialize while still collaborating through well‑defined interfaces (API contracts, platform service contracts, shared documentation). | --- #### How the Teams Interact Today 1. **Feature Initiation** – Product & design define a new capability. 2. **Frontend** builds the UI, consuming the **Backend** APIs that expose the required data/behaviour. 3. **Backend** implements or extends the API, focusing on business rules, data validation, and response shaping. 4. When the Backend needs to **run** a new service or update its deployment pipeline, it requests resources from the **Platform** team (e.g., a new namespace, CI pipeline template, or a monitoring dashboard). 5. **Platform** provides the requested infrastructure as a self‑service offering, ensures it meets security/compliance standards, and monitors its health. 6. All three teams share a **definition of done** that includes functional testing (frontend & backend), contract testing (backend API), and operational readiness (platform checks). --- ### TL;DR Summary * **Frontend Team** – owns everything the user sees and interacts with. * **Backend Team** – owns business logic and the public APIs that power the product. * **Platform Team** – owns the cloud/infra, CI/CD, observability, and reliability tooling that runs the Backend services (and any other services the company builds). The structure emerged in three logical steps: 1️⃣ One full‑stack team → 2️⃣ Split into Frontend & Backend → 3️⃣ Carved out a Platform team from Backend to take over infrastructure responsibilities. Since that final split, each team operates within a well‑defined domain, enabling the organization to scale efficiently while keeping the system stable and maintainable.
